backxwash.bio:
Zambian-Canadian rapper and producer Ashanti Mutinta, known as Backxwash, built her career in Montréal by pushing hip-hop into much harsher territory than conventional rap production usually allows. After earlier independent releases, her 2020 album God Has Nothing To Do With This Leave Him Out Of It fused distorted guitars, industrial noise, doom-metal weight and confrontational rap with writing about faith, identity and survival. The record won the 2020 Polaris Music Prize, bringing a fiercely experimental, independently released album to one of Canada's most visible music institutions.

That breakthrough became the first part of a trilogy. I Lie Here Buried with My Rings and My Dresses followed in 2021, and His Happiness Shall Come First Even Though We Are Suffering arrived in 2022, extending the project's intense mixture of horror imagery, spirituality, trauma and self-interrogation. Backxwash's production treats abrasion as an expressive tool rather than decoration: guitars, blown-out drums, samples and dense vocal layers create a sound that can move between rap, industrial music and metal without settling comfortably inside any one scene.

The 2025 album Only Dust Remains opened a new phase after that trilogy, broadening the sonic palette while keeping the emotional directness that defined the earlier work. Backxwash matters in Canadian music because her Polaris win demonstrated that uncompromising experimental rap could occupy the centre of national critical conversation without softening its sound or subject matter. Her catalogue has helped make Montréal's underground hip-hop landscape feel connected to metal, noise and electronic music as much as to rap orthodoxy.
backxwash.directory_summary: Montréal-based Zambian-Canadian rapper and producer Backxwash makes one of the country's most uncompromising forms of experimental hip-hop, combining rap with industrial noise, doom-metal weight and intensely personal writing. God Has Nothing To Do With This Leave Him Out Of It won the 2020 Polaris Music Prize, launching a trilogy that explored identity, spirituality and survival. Her 2025 album Only Dust Remains opened a broader new phase without abandoning the emotional force that made the earlier work distinctive.
album_titles: God Has Nothing To Do With This Leave Him Out Of It
I Lie Here Buried with My Rings and My Dresses
His Happiness Shall Come First Even Though We Are Suffering

charlotte day wilson.bio:
Toronto singer-songwriter, producer and engineer Charlotte Day Wilson emerged from the city's collaborative jazz, soul and alternative-R&B community with a deliberately self-contained approach to making records. Classically trained on piano and briefly a saxophone student at Dalhousie University, she began releasing solo music in the mid-2010s after earlier band work. The 2016 song "Work" became an early signature, pairing her low, resonant voice with sparse production, while the Stone Woman EP deepened a slow-burning style built around restraint, atmosphere and unusually tactile vocal arrangements.

Her 2021 debut album ALPHA expanded that language through gospel, folk, soul and adult-contemporary influences while bringing collaborators including BADBADNOTGOOD, Daniel Caesar and Syd into a record that still felt firmly authored by Wilson. She released the album through her own Stone Woman Music imprint, reinforcing the independence that has shaped both her creative and business decisions. Cyan Blue followed in 2024 with a lighter, more open production palette and received a GRAMMY nomination for Best Engineered Album, Non-Classical, recognition that also highlighted the technical side of Wilson's work in a field where women remain underrepresented behind the console.

Wilson's importance to contemporary Canadian R&B is tied as much to process as to sound. She has become a trusted collaborator for artists including Kaytranada, Daniel Caesar, Nelly Furtado and BADBADNOTGOOD while maintaining ownership-focused, independent infrastructure around her own catalogue. That combination of songwriting, production, engineering and entrepreneurship gives her a distinct place in Toronto music: not simply a featured voice within the city's scene, but one of the artists helping define how a modern Canadian R&B career can be built and controlled from the studio outward.
charlotte day wilson.directory_summary: Toronto singer-songwriter, producer and engineer Charlotte Day Wilson has become a central figure in the city's alternative-R&B ecosystem through the sparse breakthrough "Work," the Stone Woman EP and albums ALPHA and Cyan Blue. Her deep, restrained vocal style sits alongside hands-on production and engineering, while collaborations with Kaytranada, Daniel Caesar and BADBADNOTGOOD connect her across Toronto's soul, jazz and beat scenes. Releasing through her own Stone Woman Music imprint also makes creative ownership part of her artistic identity.

the halluci nation.bio:
The Halluci Nation grew out of the Ottawa project A Tribe Called Red, whose members built a new kind of Indigenous club space through the Electric Pow Wow parties launched at Babylon nightclub in 2007. Their music brought powwow singing and drumming into direct conversation with electronic dance music, hip-hop, dubstep and bass production, not as a novelty crossover but as a contemporary Indigenous cultural language. The self-titled debut and Nation II Nation carried that sound from Ottawa parties to international stages, with Nation II Nation reaching the 2013 Polaris Music Prize Short List.

We Are the Halluci Nation expanded the idea into a larger political and collaborative statement. The album brought together voices including John Trudell, Tanya Tagaq, Lido Pimienta, Yasiin Bey, Saul Williams and Black Bear Singers, and it reached the 2017 Polaris Short List. The project's performances likewise made space for Indigenous dancers, singers and visual language within festival and awards-show settings that had rarely centred them. After lineup changes, Bear Witness and Tim "2oolman" Hill reintroduced the project as The Halluci Nation, taking the name from Trudell's concept of a global community grounded in a deeper sense of human connection.

The Halluci Nation's significance reaches beyond genre. Their work helped establish a widely visible model for Indigenous artists using electronic production on their own cultural and political terms, while the JUNO Awards has cited the group among artists who fuse contemporary forms with Indigenous narratives, instruments and singing traditions. The later album One More Saturday Night turned back toward the communal roots of the Electric Pow Wow era, connecting the current duo to the Ottawa gatherings that started the movement. Across those phases, the project has made dance music function as celebration, resistance, futurism and community-building at the same time.
the halluci nation.directory_summary: Ottawa's The Halluci Nation, formerly A Tribe Called Red, transformed the Electric Pow Wow parties into an internationally influential fusion of powwow singing and drumming, electronic production, hip-hop and bass music. Nation II Nation and We Are the Halluci Nation both reached the Polaris Short List, while collaborations with John Trudell, Tanya Tagaq, Lido Pimienta and Black Bear Singers expanded the project into a broader Indigenous cultural statement. Their work made club music a space for celebration, resistance and Indigenous futurism.
